title: Questions
text:
Prerequisites


What are the course prerequisites?

Like all courses at IIT Gandhinagar, the course has no formal prerequisites. It assumes a basic understanding of programming in Python.



What is the prerequisite exam?

An exam designed to make sure you have the background needed for the course.



How can I prepare for the prerequisite exam?

Your undergraduate course material should be enough.



What happens if I do not clear the prerequisite exam?

You will not be allowed to take the course.



What does “clear” the exam mean?

As in all courses at IIT Gandhinagar, the instructor decides the cut-off, and you must score above it. The cut-off is not revealed to students beforehand.

title: Questions
text:
Laptops


Can I use my laptop or phone in class?

No, not for any reason, unless it is a lab session where the instructor has explicitly allowed laptops.

title: Questions
text:
Quizzes


What if I miss a quiz?


The quiz is marked 0.
The best 3 of 4 rule is designed for such cases.




Are the quizzes and the end-semester exam open book? Can I carry notes?

No. Exams and quizzes are closed book, and you may not carry notes.



When do I get my answer sheets back?

Within 4 to 5 working days.



Is there a mid-semester or end-semester exam?

Two of the four quizzes are held in the mid-semester and end-semester exam slots. The other two are held during the semester.



Are the quizzes multiple-choice or written?

They may contain both multiple-choice and written questions.

title: Questions
text:
Assignments


What if I miss an assignment?

There are no extensions for assignments.



I have a doubt about an assignment. Whom should I ask?

Ask on the #assignments channel on Slack. If you get no response within 2 days, write to the course instructor.



I do not know Python. Can I write assignments in another language?

No. Assignments must be in Python.



How are assignments evaluated?

Each assignment is followed by a viva. The TAs first check the code against the submission; any change from the submitted code is not allowed and leads to a warning. The TAs then run the code and ask a few questions: about 75% on the assignment and about 25% on the theory behind the concepts it covers.
The marks are split as follows: the code runs correctly and solves the problem (50%); questions on the assignment and your understanding of the code (25%); code quality (12.5%); questions on the theory (12.5%).



Are assignments individual or group?

Group. All team members get the same grade for the assignment.

title: Questions
text:
Attendance


What is the attendance policy?

See Attendance and Leave on the Assessment page.

title: Questions
text:
Auditing


Can I audit the course?

You are free to attend the lectures. However, with a limited number of TAs and a large number of students, your submissions cannot be graded, and you cannot formally contribute to a team’s assignments.

title: Questions
text:
Computational resources


Will we get cloud credits?

Google has typically provided cloud credits, which are more than enough for the assignments. This section was to be updated once the credits were available.

title: Exposition assignment
text:
Deliverables

A 4-minute video explaining and demonstrating the assigned topic.
A blog article with explanations, code snippets and screenshots, hosted on GitHub Pages.

title: Exposition assignment
text:
Video
You are free to structure the video to suit your topic and presentation style. One suggested template:

Introduction (30 s): briefly introduce the tool, library or framework and/or the problem it solves.
Key features (1 min): highlight its important capabilities.
Demonstration (2 min): show a hands-on example.
Conclusion (30 s): summarise its strengths and potential use cases.

Formatting:

Resolution: a high-quality screen recording (1080p recommended).
Audio: clear, with minimal background noise.
Narration: concise and well paced.
Visuals: a mix of slides and live demonstrations.
Background music: royalty-free music may be used.
Editing: tools such as Canva may be useful.

Each team submits:

Video link: uploaded to a public platform such as YouTube or Drive.
YouTube title: clear and relevant to the topic.
YouTube description: a brief summary of the content with relevant links.
Chapters: timestamps for the sections of the video.

title: Exposition assignment
text:
Blog article
A suggested organisation; your topic may not need all of these, or may need more. Adapt where necessary.

Title: clear and descriptive.
Introduction: an overview of the tool and its purpose.
Installation and setup: steps to install and configure it.
Key features and explanation: its main functionality.
Code examples: working examples with explanations.
Screenshots: to illustrate important points.
Use cases: practical applications.
Conclusion: summary and final thoughts.
References and further reading: links to official documentation or tutorials.

Hosting on GitHub Pages:

Use a Jupyter notebook, a Markdown-based site (for example Jekyll), Quarto or similar.
Make sure the formatting is correct and the layout works on mobile.
Link all necessary files in the repository.

title: Exposition assignment
text:
Grading rubric

Video clarity and structure3Clear audio and video, structured explanation

title: Exposition assignment
text:
Submission

Upload the video to a public platform (YouTube or Drive) and share the link.
Provide the YouTube title, description and chapter timestamps.
Provide the GitHub Pages link to the blog article.
Submit all details on the course submission portal.

The deadline was announced on Slack; the tentative deadline was 25 February 2025 (see Dates).
Plagiarism will not be tolerated. Make sure your explanations are original and insightful.

Probability, Statistics and Data Visualization
ES 114 · IIT Gandhinagar · Semester II, 2024–25
ES 114 is a first-year undergraduate course. It starts with the Python data stack (NumPy, pandas and Matplotlib), then builds up probability from sets: conditional probability and Bayes' theorem, random variables and their distributions, expectation and moments, joint distributions, sums and transformations of random variables, the law of large numbers, the multivariate normal distribution and principal component analysis.

What if I miss a quiz?It is marked 0. The best three of four quizzes count, which is designed for such cases, and there are no makeup quizzes for any reason. The mid-semester and end-semester exams count as quizzes.
Are quizzes open book?No. Quizzes and exams are closed book, and you may not carry notes. They may mix multiple-choice and written questions.
How are assignments done and graded?In groups of three, in Python, with no extensions. Each is followed by a viva: code that runs and solves the problem 50%, questions on the assignment and your code 25%, code quality 12.5%, theory 12.5%. See Assignments.
Can I use my laptop or phone in class?No, except in a lab session where the instructor has explicitly allowed laptops.

title: Uniform Distribution Transformation

import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

%matplotlib inline
%config InlineBackend.figure_format = 'retina'
a, b = 1, 3
num_samples = 100000

uniform_dist = torch.distributions.Uniform(a, b)
X_samples = uniform_dist.sample((num_samples,))

Y_samples = X_samples ** 2

y_values = torch.linspace(a**2, b**2, 500)
f_Y = 1 / (2 * torch.sqrt(y_values) * (b - a))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6), sharey=True)

axes[0].hist(X_samples.numpy(), bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="Empirical PDF")
axes[0].axhline(1 / (b - a), color='r', linestyle='--', label="Theoretical PDF")
axes[0].set_xlabel("X ~ Uniform(a, b)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
axes[0].set_title("PDF of Uniform(a, b)")
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].grid()

axes[1].hist(Y_samples.numpy(), bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="Empirical PDF")
axes[1].plot(y_values.numpy(), f_Y.numpy(), 'r-', label="Theoretical PDF")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Y = X^2")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Density")
axes[1].set_title("Transformation of Uniform(a, b) via Y = X^2")
axes[1].legend()
axes[1].grid()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
\(Y = X^2 \Rightarrow X = \sqrt{Y}\) or \(X = -\sqrt{Y}\)
Since \(X \in [a, b]\) and \(a > 0\), only the positive root is valid.
\[
f_Y(y) = f_X(x(y)) \cdot \left|\frac{dx}{dy}\right| = f_X(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}
\] And since \(f_X(x) = \frac{1}{b - a}\) (for uniform),
\[
f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{b - a} \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}, \quad \text{for } y \in [a^2, b^2]
\]
\[
f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{2(b - a)\sqrt{y}}, \quad y \in [a^2, b^2]
\]

title: Uniform Distribution Transformation
text:
Exponentional RV
\[
f_X(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x \ge 0
\]
\[
F_X(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}
\]
\[
F_X^{-1}(u) = -\frac{\ln(1 - u)}{\lambda}
\]

lambda_ = 1.0
n_samples = 10000

# Sample from Uniform(0,1)
u = torch.rand(n_samples)

# Apply inverse CDF of exponential
samples = -torch.log(1 - u) / lambda_

# True distribution using torch.distributions
exp_dist = torch.distributions.Exponential(rate=lambda_)

x_vals = torch.linspace(0, 6, 100)
pdf_vals = exp_dist.log_prob(x_vals).exp()  # f_X(x) = λ e^(-λx)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.hist(samples.numpy(), bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="Inverse CDF Samples")
plt.plot(x_vals.numpy(), pdf_vals.numpy(), 'r-', label="True Exponential PDF")
plt.title("Inverse Transform Sampling using PyTorch")
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("Density")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
